title: How does financial literacy affect financial behavior over the life cycle? Evidence from Filipino households
authors: Cacnio, F. C.; Romarate, M. E.
tldr: Examines the effects of financial literacy on budgeting, cash-flow management, borrowing, retirement planning, and insurance behaviors across different age groups in the Philippines.
problem_and_motivation: While previous studies have examined the relationship between financial literacy and financial behavior, few have done so across the life cycle in a developing-country context. Understanding how age and life stage moderate the link between financial literacy and financial behavior is essential for designing effective financial education programs.
approach: Used 2018 BSP Consumer Finance Survey data on 7,074 Filipino households to construct a Financial Literacy Index (FLI).

FLI combines two equally-weighted components: financial attitude (sub-dimensions: attitude toward money, risk attitude, time discounting) and financial aptitude (sub-dimensions: loan score, deposit score, surplus score).
Conducted OLS regressions to determine factors associated with financial literacy, including age, gender, education, income, marital status, children, and remittances.

Used logit regressions to assess how financial literacy and age affect five financial behaviors: spending-income balancing, loan payment timeliness, loan-to-income ratio, retirement/pension plans, and insurance.
Ran probit regressions as an alternative methodology to validate the findings from the logit models.
Disaggregated savings data by age group to analyze differences in total savings (deposit accounts and emergency cash).
findings: num: Young adults (18-39) have the highest financial literacy scores among the three age cohorts.
num: Female respondents have slightly lower financial aptitude and overall literacy compared to males (coeff -0.006, p<0.01).
num: Respondents with at least high school education have higher financial literacy (coeff 0.015, p<0.001 for FLI).
num: Higher financial attitude scores increase likelihood of paying loans on time (odds ratio 4.011, p<0.05).
num: Higher financial aptitude scores increase likelihood of having a pension (odds ratio 85.478, p<0.001) and insurance (46.808, p<0.001).
num: Middle-aged people (40-59) are less likely to have a loan-to-income ratio below 1 compared to young adults (odds ratio 0.280, p<0.05).
num: People with higher financial literacy are less likely to spend less than their income (odds ratio <1 for both attitude and aptitude).
num: Seniors have the highest average total savings (PhP 36,722), followed by middle-aged (PhP 15,935) and young adults (PhP 13,402).

Table 5: Determinants of financial literacy (OLS): age, gender, education, income, children, and remittances.
Table 6: Logistic regression models for five financial behaviors: spending, loan payment, borrowing, retirement, insurance.

topic_relevance.contribution_to_field: This paper provides a comprehensive empirical analysis of the relationship between financial literacy and financial behaviors across the life cycle using a large, nationally representative sample of Filipino households. It develops a Financial Literacy Index with two main components and evaluates its relationship with five distinct financial behaviors: spending-income balancing, loan payment, borrowing, retirement planning, and insurance. The study reveals that financial literacy components have differential effects on behaviors: financial attitude influences cash-flow management while financial aptitude is more strongly associated with long-term planning. It finds that young adults have the highest financial literacy but the lowest savings, highlighting a disconnect between knowledge and saving behavior. The paper provides evidence-based policy recommendations for designing financial education programs tailored to different life stages in the Philippine context.
directly_justifies: Young adults (18-39) have the highest financial literacy but lowest average savings (PhP 13,402).
Financial aptitude strongly predicts having a pension (odds 85.5) and insurance (46.8).
Higher financial literacy is associated with lower likelihood of spending within one's income.
Middle-aged people are less likely than young adults to have a loan-to-income ratio below 1.
Financial education programs should be tailored to life stages, with enhanced emphasis on retirement planning.
limits: Study relies on 2018 BSP CFS data which may not reflect post-pandemic financial behaviors.
Financial literacy is measured through a constructed index that may not capture all dimensions of financial awareness.
Assumption of causality from financial literacy to behavior is not proven; reverse causality is possible.
Data on savings may be underreported by respondents.
topic_relevance.topic_mapping_rationale: All 14 topic domains in the taxonomy were systematically scanned. Domain 1 (Filipino Young Professionals) received high relevance as the study explicitly disaggregates by age groups (young adult 18-39). Domain 2 (Culturally Specific Financial Practices) received high relevance — based on a large Filipino household sample. Domain 3 (Expense Categorization) was low: groups financial activities but no formal framework. Domain 13 (Savings and Debt Management) received medium relevance: provides savings and debt data but no PFMS system design. Domains 4 (Landscape of Existing Personal Finance Systems), 5 (Behavioral Profiles), 6 (Predictive Modeling), 7 (Budgeting Strategies), 8 (Anomaly Detection), 9 (Mobile-First Design), 10 (Data Privacy), 11 (Engagement Dynamics), 12 (Evaluation Frameworks), and 14 (ML & Synthetic Data) were considered and rejected as the paper does not address any system design, algorithmic, or evaluation aspect of personal finance management systems. It is a study of financial literacy effects on behavior, not a system or algorithm proposal.

limitations: Uses 2018 BSP CFS data; may not reflect post-pandemic financial behaviors.
Financial literacy index may not capture all dimensions of awareness and understanding.
Causality assumed from literacy to behavior; reverse causality not addressed.
Savings data is self-reported and may be underestimated.
Sample sizes for some logit regressions (e.g., loan payments) are much smaller (n=1,743) than the full sample (n=7,074).
remember_this: Young adults have the highest financial literacy but the lowest savings among age groups.
Financial aptitude strongly predicts having a pension and insurance plans.
Higher financial literacy is associated with lower likelihood of spending within income.
Financial education programs should be designed to target specific life stages.
Middle-aged people tend to have higher loan-to-income ratios than young adults.
